pride-and-prejudice: In Hertfordshire, the Bennet family has five unmarried daughters and an estate that will pass to a male cousin, so marriage is a pressing matter. When the wealthy, good-natured Mr. Bingley rents nearby Netherfield, he brings his proud friend Mr. Darcy, who promptly offends the sharp-witted Elizabeth Bennet at a local ball. As visits and gossip multiply, Elizabeth forms firm opinions of Darcy and of the charming officer Mr. Wickham, while her gentle elder sister Jane falls for Bingley.

Austen turns a small world of drawing rooms into a sharp study of judgement, class and self-knowledge. Her famous irony, brisk dialogue and gallery of comic figures, such as the pompous clergyman Mr. Collins, keep the pages lively, while beneath the comedy lies a serious look at how women's futures depended on money and marriage. Readers return to it for Elizabeth herself, one of the most likeable and independent heroines in fiction, and for the pleasure of watching two clever people learn to see clearly.

Austen drafted an early version under the title First Impressions in the late 1790s. Revised, it was published anonymously by Thomas Egerton in January 1813 as the work of the author of Sense and Sensibility. It was well received at once and has never gone out of print. The novel has inspired many film and television versions, stage productions and many modern retellings.
great-expectations: Pip, an orphan raised by his harsh sister and her kind husband, the blacksmith Joe Gargery, lives on the misty marshes of Kent. One evening in a churchyard he is seized by an escaped convict and frightened into helping him. Soon afterwards he is summoned to Satis House, home of the strange, reclusive Miss Havisham, where he meets her proud young ward Estella and begins to feel ashamed of his common life. When a mysterious benefactor gives him the means to become a gentleman in London, Pip leaves the forge behind, and the novel follows what that change makes of him.

Narrated by an older Pip, the book explores snobbery, guilt, loyalty and the difference between real worth and social rank. Dickens mixes dark comedy, Gothic atmosphere and deep tenderness, and his characters, from the eccentric clerk Wemmick to the lawyer Jaggers, are unforgettable. It is often seen as one of his most tightly constructed and personal novels, and its honest portrait of ambition still speaks to readers.

Great Expectations first appeared in weekly parts in Dickens's own magazine All the Year Round from December 1860 to August 1861 and was published in book form in 1861. Dickens famously revised the final chapter after a friend's advice, and both versions are still discussed. The novel has been adapted many times for cinema, television, radio and the stage.
wuthering-heights: In 1801 a tenant named Lockwood visits his landlord, the brooding Heathcliff, at a remote farmhouse called Wuthering Heights on the Yorkshire moors. Puzzled by the hostile household and unsettled by a night of strange dreams, he asks the housekeeper Nelly Dean for its history. Her story goes back a generation, to the day old Mr. Earnshaw brought home a ragged foundling child, and traces the fierce bond that grew between that boy and Earnshaw's daughter Catherine, and the resentments it stirred in the Earnshaw and Linton families.

The novel is famous for its layered narration, its untamed landscape and the sheer intensity of its emotions. Love, revenge, cruelty and social ambition are bound together, and Brontë refuses to make her characters simply good or bad, which is why readers still argue about them. Its blend of realism, poetry and something close to the supernatural makes it unlike any other Victorian novel, and it rewards rereading.

Emily Brontë published the book in 1847 under the pen name Ellis Bell, in the same set of volumes as her sister Anne's Agnes Grey. Early reviewers were often shocked by its violence and passion. Emily died the following year, and her sister Charlotte prepared a new edition in 1850. Its reputation has grown steadily, and it has inspired numerous films, television series, operas, songs and stage adaptations.
the-adventures-of-huckleberry-finn: Huck Finn, first met in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, tells his own story in his own voice. Uneasy with the widow who is trying to civilise him and threatened by his violent, drunken father, Huck fakes his death and escapes to an island in the Mississippi. There he meets Jim, a man fleeing slavery, and the two set off downriver on a raft. Their journey through the pre-Civil War South brings feuds, small towns and con men, and forces Huck to question everything he has been taught.

Twain's use of everyday spoken American English, with its regional dialects, was groundbreaking and gave the book its humour and life. Beneath the adventure lies a searching satire of hypocrisy, racism and the moral blindness of respectable society, centred on Huck's growing friendship with Jim. The novel's frequent use of racial slurs and its portrayal of Jim continue to spark debate in classrooms, part of why it remains so widely discussed.

The book was first published in Britain in December 1884 and in the United States in early 1885. It quickly drew controversy, and some libraries removed it soon after publication for what they saw as coarse language. Over time it came to be regarded as one of the great American novels, influencing generations of writers, and it has been adapted for film, television, musical theatre and retold from new perspectives.
hamlet: At the castle of Elsinore in Denmark, Prince Hamlet is grieving his father, the late king, and struggling with his mother Gertrude's hasty marriage to his uncle Claudius, who now wears the crown. When guards report a ghost on the battlements, Hamlet confronts it and learns of a terrible crime. Resolving to act, he puts on a show of madness, leaving the court, the scheming counsellor Polonius, and his daughter Ophelia uncertain what is real as the tension mounts.

Hamlet is a play about thinking as much as doing. Its hero weighs revenge, conscience, death and the meaning of action in speeches that remain among the most celebrated in English. Shakespeare mixes political intrigue, family conflict, dark wit and a play within the play, and offers a central character so complex that every generation and every actor finds someone new in him.

Written around 1599 to 1601, the play drew on an old Scandinavian legend of a prince named Amleth. It first appeared in print in a short quarto of 1603, followed by a fuller text in 1604 and the version in the First Folio of 1623. It is Shakespeare's longest play and among the most performed works in the world, inspiring countless stage productions, films, operas, novels and spin-offs such as Tom Stoppard's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead.
the-wealth-of-nations: Adam Smith's full title, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, states his question plainly: what makes some countries rich? His answer begins with the division of labour, famously illustrated by a pin factory in which workers who specialise produce far more than any one person could alone. From there he examines money, prices, wages, profit and rent, how capital is accumulated, the history of European economic development, and the role and revenue of government.

A central theme is that people pursuing their own interests within fair rules and competitive markets can, without intending it, benefit society as a whole, an idea Smith links to his image of an invisible hand. He attacks mercantilism, the policy of hoarding gold and protecting trade with monopolies and tariffs, yet he also warns of merchants conspiring against the public and treats defence, justice and public works as duties of the state. Its clear prose remains surprisingly readable.

Smith, a Scottish moral philosopher already known for The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), spent around a decade on the book, which was published in London in March 1776. It was revised through several editions in his lifetime and shaped the work of later economists such as David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus. It is still cited across the political spectrum and is widely regarded as a founding text of modern economics.
principles-of-political-economy: John Stuart Mill's Principles of Political Economy sets out to cover the whole field of economics as it stood in the mid-nineteenth century. Building on Adam Smith and David Ricardo, it moves through production, distribution, exchange, economic progress and the influence of government. Mill explains labour, capital and land, wages and profits, value and money, international trade and taxation, always connecting theory to practical questions of policy.

Its most distinctive idea is that the laws of production are fixed by nature, while the distribution of wealth depends on human institutions and can therefore be changed. This allowed Mill to defend markets while seriously considering reforms in property, inheritance and land, and to look hopefully at cooperative associations of workers. He also argues that a stationary state, in which population and capital stop growing, need not be a misfortune and might leave more room for human improvement, a passage that sounds strikingly modern. His style is patient, balanced and humane.

First published in two volumes in 1848, the book went through several editions in Mill's lifetime, and he revised it substantially along the way. He acknowledged the strong influence of Harriet Taylor, later his wife, especially on the chapter about the future of the working classes. For decades it was the standard economics text in English-speaking universities, until Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics (1890) took its place.
the-scarlet-letter: In seventeenth-century Puritan Boston, a young woman named Hester Prynne stands on the scaffold holding her infant daughter, Pearl, condemned to wear a scarlet letter A on her gown as a mark of adultery. She refuses to name the child's father. Watching from the crowd is a stranger, in fact her long-absent husband, who takes the name Roger Chillingworth and quietly sets out to discover the man who wronged him. The novel follows Hester, Pearl and the people around them over the following years as secrets work on everyone involved.

Hawthorne explores sin, guilt, shame, hypocrisy and the harshness of a community that punishes in public while hiding its own failings. Hester's quiet strength and dignity make her one of the great heroines of American literature, and the novel's rich symbolism, centred on the letter itself, invites many readings. Its brooding, psychological style still feels intense and modern.

The book was published in Boston in 1850 and made Hawthorne's reputation almost overnight. It opens with a long autobiographical sketch, The Custom-House, describing his time working in Salem, where he claims to have found the letter. Hawthorne was himself descended from a judge in the Salem witch trials, and his novel is often read as a reckoning with New England's Puritan past. It has been adapted for film, television, opera and the stage.
on-the-origin-of-species: Charles Darwin argues that living species are not fixed but have changed over immense periods of time, and that the main force behind this change is natural selection. He begins with something familiar to his readers, the way breeders improve pigeons, dogs and crops by choosing which animals and plants reproduce. He then shows how variation, inheritance and the struggle for existence in nature produce a similar effect without any breeder at all, and goes on to examine instinct, hybrids, the fossil record, geographical distribution and the similarities between living things.

Darwin called his book one long argument, and its strength lies in how patiently he gathers evidence, anticipates objections and admits difficulties. Writing for a general educated audience rather than specialists, he uses clear prose and countless examples from his own observations, including those made during his voyage on HMS Beagle. Reading it today shows how a revolutionary idea was built step by step.

The book was published by John Murray in London on 24 November 1859, a year after Darwin's and Alfred Russel Wallace's ideas were jointly presented to the Linnean Society. It caused immediate scientific and religious debate. Darwin revised it through six editions, adding the phrase survival of the fittest, borrowed from Herbert Spencer, in 1869. It became the foundation of modern biology.
the-call-of-the-wild: Buck, a large and powerful dog, lives a comfortable life on Judge Miller's estate in California's Santa Clara Valley. But it is the 1890s, gold has been found in the Klondike, and strong dogs are in demand. Stolen by a gardener's helper and sold north, Buck is thrown into the harsh world of the Yukon, where he must learn the law of club and fang, pull sleds through snow and survive among rival dogs and masters of very different kinds.

Told largely from Buck's point of view, the short novel is an adventure story with deeper questions about civilisation, instinct and survival. Jack London writes with vivid physical detail about cold, hunger and endurance, and he shows how an animal shaped by comfort discovers older, wilder impulses within himself. It is gripping for young readers and thought-provoking for adults, especially in its depiction of how humans treat the animals they depend on.

London had travelled to the Klondike himself during the gold rush of 1897, and that experience fed directly into the book. The Call of the Wild was serialised in The Saturday Evening Post and published as a book in 1903, and it brought him wide fame. He later wrote White Fang (1906) as a kind of companion piece. The story has been adapted many times for film, television and animation.
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles: Dr. Mortimer arrives at 221B Baker Street with an old family manuscript and a worrying story. Sir Charles Baskerville has been found dead on the grounds of his Devon home, and near the body were the footprints of an enormous hound. According to legend, a demonic dog has haunted the Baskervilles for generations. With the young heir, Sir Henry, about to take up his inheritance, Sherlock Holmes sends Dr. Watson to Dartmoor to watch over him, and Watson finds himself among mysterious neighbours, an escaped convict and the bleak, treacherous moor itself.

The novel blends detective fiction with Gothic horror, setting Holmes's cool reasoning against superstition and fear. Much of the story is told through Watson's reports and diary, which gives him a larger role than usual and builds suspense skilfully. The atmosphere of the moor, with its mists, mires and ancient stone huts, is one of the most memorable settings in crime fiction, and the puzzle remains satisfying for new readers.

Conan Doyle had killed off Holmes in 1893, but this story, set before the detective's apparent death, brought him back. It ran in The Strand Magazine from 1901 to 1902 and was published as a book in 1902, to great popular enthusiasm. Doyle credited his friend Bertram Fletcher Robinson with suggesting the idea. It is among the most adapted Holmes stories, on film, radio, television and stage.
the-house-by-the-medlar-tree: In Aci Trezza, a fishing village on the coast of Sicily near Catania, the Toscano family, nicknamed the Malavoglia, live in the house by the medlar tree. The household is led by the old patriarch Padron 'Ntoni, who speaks in proverbs and believes in hard work and family unity. Hoping to improve their fortunes, the family buys a cargo of lupins on credit and sends it out on their boat, the Provvidenza. When the venture goes badly wrong, they are left with a debt, and must struggle to keep their home and honour as the modern world presses in.

Verga tells the story almost without a narrator's voice, letting the gossip, sayings and viewpoints of the villagers carry the narrative. This choral, impersonal style was a bold innovation and is central to the movement known as verismo. The book is a moving portrait of poverty, dignity, change and the pull between tradition and the wish to escape, and its humane attention to ordinary people still feels fresh.

I Malavoglia was published in Milan in 1881 as the first part of a planned cycle about society's defeated, of which Verga completed only one further novel. It was poorly received at first but is now regarded as a masterpiece of Italian literature. It has been translated under this English title and loosely inspired Luchino Visconti's film La terra trema (1948).
walden: On 4 July 1845, Henry David Thoreau moved into a small cabin he had built himself beside Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts, on land owned by his friend Ralph Waldo Emerson. He lived there for about two years, and Walden is his account of the experiment, compressed into the cycle of a single year. He begins with a detailed look at what he actually needed in food, shelter and clothing, then turns to reading, solitude, visitors, his bean field, the animals of the woods and the changing life of the pond through the seasons.

The book is part nature writing, part philosophy and part sharp social criticism. Thoreau questions the busy, debt-driven lives of his neighbours and asks what it means to live deliberately and simply. His prose moves from precise observation to bold, playful aphorism, and readers today often find his reflections on consumption, work, technology and attention surprisingly relevant.

Walden was published by Ticknor and Fields in Boston in 1854 after several years of revision, and it sold modestly at first. Its reputation grew steadily after Thoreau's death in 1862. During his stay at the pond he was briefly jailed for refusing to pay a poll tax, an episode behind his essay on civil disobedience. Walden is now seen as a founding text of American environmental thought and continues to inspire writers, naturalists and advocates of simple living.
the-railway-children: Roberta, called Bobbie, Peter and Phyllis live a happy, comfortable life in London until one evening their father is taken away by two strange men. Their mother will not explain what has happened, and the family must suddenly move to a modest country house called Three Chimneys, where Mother writes stories to pay the bills. With little money and plenty of free time, the children are drawn to the nearby railway line, where they make friends with the porter Perks, wave to an old gentleman on a passing train and find themselves caught up in a series of adventures and rescues.

Nesbit writes about children with warmth, humour and respect, letting them be brave, quarrelsome, generous and sometimes foolish. The book deals gently with poverty, injustice and kindness between strangers, and it shows how small acts of courage can change things. Its sense of community and hope makes it a favourite for families reading aloud.

The story was first serialised in The London Magazine in 1905 and published as a book in 1906. Nesbit, a founding member of the Fabian Society, was already a successful children's author, known for The Story of the Treasure Seekers and Five Children and It. The Railway Children has been adapted several times for film, television, radio and the stage, including a much-loved film version.
treasure-island: Jim Hawkins helps his mother run the Admiral Benbow inn on the English coast, until an old sea captain named Billy Bones takes a room and brings trouble with him. After a visit from sinister former shipmates, Jim finds himself holding a map that leads to the buried treasure of the notorious pirate Captain Flint. With Squire Trelawney and Dr. Livesey, he sets sail on the Hispaniola under the stern Captain Smollett, with a crew that includes a cheerful, one-legged sea cook named Long John Silver.

Told mostly by Jim, the novel is a classic coming-of-age adventure full of suspense, danger and quick changes of fortune. Stevenson writes in clean, vigorous prose, and his portrait of Silver, charming, clever and impossible to pin down, is one of the great characters in fiction. Beneath the excitement the book raises questions about loyalty, greed and how a boy learns to judge the adults around him.

Stevenson began the story in 1881 after drawing an imaginary island map with his young stepson. It was serialised in the magazine Young Folks under the pen name Captain George North, then published as a book in 1883. Much of our popular image of pirates, from treasure maps marked with an X to parrots on shoulders, owes a great deal to it, and it has been adapted countless times for screen, stage and radio.
sense-and-sensibility: When Mr. Dashwood dies, his estate at Norland Park passes to his son from a first marriage, and the son's selfish wife, Fanny, persuades him to give almost nothing to his stepmother and half-sisters. Mrs. Dashwood and her daughters Elinor, Marianne and young Margaret move to a modest cottage in Devonshire, offered by a cousin, Sir John Middleton. Calm, self-controlled Elinor has grown attached to Fanny's brother Edward Ferrars, while passionate Marianne is swept off her feet by the dashing John Willoughby, and is admired from a distance by the quiet Colonel Brandon.

The novel contrasts two ways of meeting the world, careful judgement and open feeling, without simply declaring one right. Austen's wit is already sharp, especially in her portraits of greedy relatives and gossiping neighbours, and she shows clearly how money, inheritance law and social expectation shaped women's choices. The bond between the two sisters gives the book its emotional heart.

Austen began an early version, called Elinor and Marianne, in the 1790s. Sense and Sensibility was her first published novel, issued by Thomas Egerton in 1811 and credited only to a lady. It sold well enough to encourage the publication of Pride and Prejudice two years later. It has since been adapted for film, television and the stage and has inspired modern retellings.
dubliners: Dubliners is a collection of fifteen short stories set in Dublin in the early years of the twentieth century. Joyce arranged them to move roughly from childhood through adolescence and adulthood to public life. A boy reflects on the death of an old priest, a young woman weighs the chance to leave for a new life abroad, a clerk is humiliated at work, and a group of political canvassers gather on a wet October day. The collection ends with The Dead, the longest story, set at a family party during the Christmas season.

Joyce writes in a precise, restrained style that lets small details reveal a great deal. Many stories turn on a sudden moment of insight that Joyce called an epiphany, and many of his characters feel trapped by poverty, religion, family duty or politics. The book is an unsentimental yet compassionate portrait of a city and a nation, and it is often the best way to begin reading Joyce.

Joyce completed most of the stories by 1907, but publishers hesitated for years over their frank language and references to real people and places, and one Dublin printer destroyed the sheets of an edition in 1912. The collection was finally published in London in 1914. It is now considered a landmark of the modern short story, and The Dead was filmed by John Huston in 1987.
beowulf: Beowulf is a long poem in Old English, set not in England but in the Scandinavian world of the Danes and the Geats. For years the great hall of Heorot, built by the Danish king Hrothgar, has been terrorised by the monster Grendel, who attacks by night. A young Geatish warrior, Beowulf, sails across the sea with his companions to offer help. The poem follows his struggles against Grendel and then Grendel's mother in her underwater lair, and later, many years on, against a fire-breathing dragon threatening his own people.

Beyond the monster fights, the poem reflects on loyalty, generosity, fame, kingship and the shortness of human life. It is written in alliterative verse rich in kennings, compound phrases such as whale-road for the sea, and it weaves in older stories and feuds that deepen its sense of history. Its mix of pagan heroic values and Christian outlook makes it a fascinating window into early medieval thought.

The poem survives in a single manuscript copied around the year 1000 and damaged in a fire in 1731. Its date of composition is still debated. It was first printed in 1815, and J. R. R. Tolkien's 1936 lecture helped establish it as a work of literary art. It has been translated many times, notably by Seamus Heaney in 1999, and retold in novels, films, comics and opera.
the-tempest: Twelve years before the play begins, Prospero, the rightful Duke of Milan, was overthrown by his brother Antonio with the help of Alonso, King of Naples, and set adrift with his little daughter Miranda. They reached a remote island, where Prospero studied magic and took command of the airy spirit Ariel and the island's resentful native, Caliban. Now his enemies' ship is passing nearby, and Prospero raises a storm that wrecks it and scatters its passengers across the island, setting his plans in motion.

The Tempest is a play about power, forgiveness, freedom and illusion. Prospero's control over others, especially Ariel and Caliban, has led many modern readers to see the play as a reflection on colonisation, while Miranda's first sight of other people gives it wonder and freshness. Shakespeare mixes romance, comedy, music, masque and some of his most beautiful poetry, and the play closes with an epilogue in which Prospero speaks directly to the audience.

The play was performed at court in November 1611 and first printed as the opening play of the First Folio in 1623. It is generally thought to be the last play Shakespeare wrote alone, which is why it is often read as his farewell to the theatre. Accounts of a 1609 shipwreck in Bermuda probably influenced it. It has inspired operas, ballets, music, poems, films and rewritings.
the-hunchback-of-notre-dame: The novel opens in Paris on 6 January 1482, during the riotous Festival of Fools, when the crowd crowns the deformed, deaf bell-ringer of Notre-Dame, Quasimodo, as Pope of Fools. That same day the struggling poet Pierre Gringoire is swept into the city's underworld, and all eyes turn to Esmeralda, a young street dancer who performs with her clever goat. She attracts the attention of three very different men: Quasimodo, his guardian the stern archdeacon Claude Frollo, and the handsome captain Phoebus. Their desires set in motion a tragedy that plays out around the great cathedral.

Hugo's novel is about love, obsession, cruelty and the outsider, but it is also a passionate portrait of medieval Paris and of the cathedral itself, which is almost a character in its own right. He adds long digressions on architecture, printing and history, arguing that buildings were once the books of humanity. His mix of grotesque and sublime, comedy and horror, remains powerful and very cinematic.

Published in 1831 under the French title Notre-Dame de Paris, the novel was a great success and helped spark public concern for the cathedral, which was in poor repair; a major restoration followed in the 1840s. Its English title shifted the focus to Quasimodo. It has been adapted many times, in silent and sound films, animation, ballet, opera and stage musicals.
grimm-s-fairy-tales: Grimm's Fairy Tales is the familiar name for Children's and Household Tales, a collection of folk stories gathered by the brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm. It includes tales now known around the world: Snow White, Hansel and Gretel, Rapunzel, Cinderella, Little Red Riding Hood, Rumpelstiltskin, The Frog King and many more. Alongside them are stories of clever tailors, talking animals, enchanted siblings, wicked stepmothers, poor millers and lucky fools, set in a world of forests, castles and cottages.

The tales are short, direct and often startling, with sudden cruelty, magic and justice. Their themes of courage, kindness, cunning, hunger and the dangers of growing up have kept them alive for over two centuries. Reading them in fuller form, rather than in softened modern versions, reveals how strange and sometimes dark they can be, and how much they say about the fears and hopes of ordinary people.

The first volume appeared in 1812 and a second followed in 1815. The brothers, scholars interested in German language and culture, gathered material from storytellers and printed sources, and Wilhelm in particular revised and polished the tales across many editions until the last in 1857. Translated into English from 1823, the tales spread widely and have shaped picture books, films, theatre and literature worldwide.
les-miserables: Les Misérables follows Jean Valjean, a man released after nineteen years in prison for stealing bread and later trying to escape. Hardened and shunned, he is transformed by an unexpected act of kindness from the Bishop of Digne and resolves to live an honest life. Yet the police inspector Javert, who believes no criminal can change, never stops hunting him. Ranging from 1815 to the Paris uprising of June 1832, the novel weaves Valjean's fate together with those of the struggling factory worker Fantine, her daughter Cosette, the scheming Thénardier family and the young idealist Marius.

Hugo's great subjects are justice and mercy, poverty and the law, and the possibility of moral rebirth. He writes on an enormous scale, pausing the story for long reflections on Waterloo, the Paris sewers, convents and the street children of the city. These digressions give the book its sense of an entire society in motion. Its compassion for the poor and its question of whether people can truly change remain as urgent as ever.

Hugo wrote much of the novel while living in political exile on Guernsey, and it appeared in 1862 in several volumes, published simultaneously in a number of countries. It was an immediate popular event. It has since been translated into many languages and adapted countless times for film, television, radio and the stage, most famously as a long-running musical.
the-great-gatsby: The Great Gatsby is narrated by Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner who moves to Long Island in the summer of 1922 to work in the bond business in New York. His neighbour in West Egg is Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire whose lavish parties draw crowds of strangers. Across the bay in fashionable East Egg live Nick's cousin Daisy and her wealthy, overbearing husband Tom Buchanan. As Nick is drawn into Gatsby's world, he discovers that the parties, the mansion and the fortune all serve a single, carefully hidden purpose rooted in Gatsby's past.

The novel explores the American Dream and its corruption, the gulf between old money and new, and the impossibility of recapturing the past. Fitzgerald's prose is compact and lyrical, full of memorable images such as the green light at the end of Daisy's dock and the brooding billboard eyes over a desolate valley of ashes. Short enough to read in an afternoon, it rewards rereading.

Published by Scribner's in April 1925, the book received mixed reviews and modest attention during Fitzgerald's lifetime, and he died believing himself largely forgotten. Its reputation grew dramatically after the Second World War, and it became a fixture of school reading in the United States. It has been adapted for film, stage, opera and graphic novels, and entered the American public domain in 2021.
the-picture-of-dorian-gray: In a London studio, the painter Basil Hallward completes a portrait of Dorian Gray, a young man of extraordinary beauty. Basil's witty friend Lord Henry Wotton fills Dorian's head with the idea that youth and pleasure are all that matter, and Dorian wishes aloud that the painting might grow old in his place. The wish seems to come true. As Dorian pursues a life of sensation and indulgence, his face stays fresh and innocent while the hidden canvas begins to record the marks of his actions.

Wilde's only novel is a gothic moral fable wrapped in the glittering talk of a drawing-room comedy. Lord Henry's epigrams sparkle on almost every page, yet the story asks serious questions about beauty, influence, conscience and the double lives people lead behind respectable surfaces. Its blend of wit, decadence and horror makes it a vivid introduction to the aesthetic movement and to late-Victorian anxieties about art and morality.

The story first appeared in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine in 1890, where many reviewers condemned it as immoral. Wilde revised and expanded it for publication as a book in 1891, adding a famous preface of aphorisms defending art for art's sake. Passages from the novel were later raised against him during his trials in 1895. It has since inspired numerous films, stage versions and television adaptations.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland: On a drowsy summer afternoon, young Alice sees a White Rabbit hurry past, checking his pocket watch, and follows him down a rabbit hole. She lands in Wonderland, a place where drinking from a bottle or nibbling a cake makes her shrink or grow, and where nothing behaves as lessons and manners have taught her to expect. She meets the grinning Cheshire Cat, the Caterpillar on his mushroom, the Mad Hatter and March Hare at their endless tea party, and finally the furious Queen of Hearts and her chaotic court.

The book delights in nonsense, puns, parodies of Victorian school poems and games of logic that collapse into absurdity. Beneath the fun lies a sharp look at the arbitrary rules of the adult world and at a child's struggle to keep her sense of self as everything around her keeps changing. Its playful language and dreamlike structure appeal to children, while adults enjoy its wit and its sly philosophical puzzles.

Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, an Oxford mathematician. The story grew out of tales he told to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boating trip in 1862, and was published in 1865 with illustrations by John Tenniel. A sequel, Through the Looking-Glass, followed in 1871. Wonderland has been endlessly adapted in animation, live-action film, theatre and art, and its characters have entered everyday language.
romeo-and-juliet: In the Italian city of Verona, the Montague and Capulet families are locked in an old and bitter feud that spills into street brawls. Romeo, a young Montague, slips into a Capulet feast and falls instantly in love with Juliet, the daughter of the house, who returns his feelings before either learns who the other is. With the help of Juliet's talkative Nurse and the well-meaning Friar Laurence, the two pursue their love in secret, while the hostility between their families, and the hot tempers of friends such as Mercutio and Juliet's cousin Tybalt, keep growing around them.

The play is about the intensity of first love and the destructive force of hatred, haste and chance. Shakespeare moves from bawdy comedy to soaring lyric poetry, as in the balcony scene, and then to tragedy, compressing the action into just a few days. Its questions about youth, family loyalty and how violence passes between generations still speak directly to modern audiences.

Written in the mid-1590s and first printed in 1597, the play drew on Arthur Brooke's narrative poem about the lovers, itself based on Italian sources. It has remained one of Shakespeare's most frequently performed works. It has inspired operas, ballets, a celebrated Broadway musical that moved the story to New York, and many films, and the names of its lovers have become a byword for romance.
the-theory-of-moral-sentiments: Adam Smith's first book asks how human beings come to make moral judgements. His answer begins with sympathy, which he describes as our capacity to imagine ourselves in another person's situation and share, to some degree, what they feel. We approve of others' feelings and actions when we can enter into them, and disapprove when we cannot. To judge our own conduct, Smith argues, we learn to view ourselves through the eyes of an imagined impartial spectator, a figure who gradually becomes the voice of conscience. From this foundation he discusses virtue, justice, beneficence, duty and the role of rules in moral life.

The book is notable for grounding ethics in social experience and emotion rather than pure reason or religious command. Smith writes with clarity and a keen eye for everyday behaviour, examining ambition, vanity, admiration for the rich and the human desire to be worthy of praise. It corrects the image of Smith as a champion of mere self-interest.

Smith published the work in 1759 while professor of moral philosophy at the University of Glasgow, and it made his reputation across Europe. It shows the influence of his friend David Hume. He revised it repeatedly, with a substantially expanded sixth edition appearing in 1790, the year of his death. Scholars continue to study how it connects with The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776.
the-theory-of-the-leisure-class: Thorstein Veblen's study looks at the wealthy not as admirable achievers but as a class whose position depends on displaying that it does not have to work. Drawing on examples from early societies to the American rich of his own day, he argues that status is won by showing off the ability to waste. He calls this conspicuous leisure, the visible avoidance of productive labour, and conspicuous consumption, the purchase of goods chiefly to impress others. These habits, he suggests, spread downward as each social group tries to imitate the one above it.

Veblen examines fashion, manners, sport, religious ritual, the household, the treatment of women and the higher learning in universities, all through this lens. His tone is dry and ironic, often describing familiar customs as if they belonged to a strange tribe, which makes the book both funny and unsettling. In an age of luxury brands and social media display, his analysis of status, envy and waste feels strikingly current.

Published in 1899, the book brought Veblen wide attention and became one of the founding texts of American institutional economics and economic sociology. Its key phrases passed into everyday language, and economists later used the term Veblen goods for products whose appeal rises with their price. It remains widely read in courses on economics, sociology and cultural history.
uncle-tom-s-cabin: The novel opens on a Kentucky farm, where the indebted Mr Shelby agrees to sell two enslaved people: Tom, a deeply religious and dignified man, and the young son of Eliza Harris. Rather than lose her child, Eliza flees north toward freedom, while Tom is carried down the Mississippi to be sold. The story follows both paths, the escape of Eliza and her husband George pursued by slave catchers, and Tom's life among new owners, including the kindly Augustine St. Clare and his saintly daughter Eva, and later the brutal planter Simon Legree.

Stowe set out to make readers feel the human cost of slavery, especially the destruction of families, and she appealed directly to Christian conscience and to mothers. Her style is emotional and openly persuasive, typical of sentimental fiction of the period. Modern readers often criticise its racial stereotypes, yet it remains essential for understanding how literature shaped public opinion on the eve of the Civil War.

Written in response to the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, the story was serialised in the antislavery paper The National Era before appearing as a book in 1852. It was enormously widely read in the United States and Britain, and was fiercely attacked in the South. Countless stage versions, often distorting its message, followed, and the name Uncle Tom later became an insult quite different from Stowe's intent.
the-importance-of-being-earnest: Jack Worthing is a respectable guardian in the country, but in London he calls himself Ernest and enjoys a freer life. His friend Algernon Moncrieff has his own escape, an invented invalid named Bunbury whose sudden illnesses excuse him from dull engagements. Jack wants to marry Algernon's cousin Gwendolen, who adores the name Ernest, but must first satisfy her formidable mother, Lady Bracknell. When Algernon visits Jack's country house pretending to be Ernest himself, and falls for Jack's young ward Cecily, the double lives begin to collide.

Subtitled A Trivial Comedy for Serious People, the play turns Victorian ideas of duty, marriage, class and respectability upside down. Wilde treats trivial matters with great seriousness and serious matters with airy indifference, and nearly every line is an epigram. Its absurd plot, involving cucumber sandwiches, a handbag and a lost identity, moves with clockwork precision. It remains one of the funniest plays in English and a model of comic dialogue.

The play opened at the St James's Theatre in London on 14 February 1895 to great success. Within weeks Wilde's legal troubles began, and after his arrest his name was removed from publicity and the run soon ended. It was published in 1899. Since then it has been revived constantly on stage and adapted for film, radio, television and opera.
the-last-of-the-mohicans: The novel is set in 1757, during the French and Indian War, in the forests of what is now upstate New York. Cora and Alice Munro, daughters of the British commander of Fort William Henry, set out to join their father, escorted by Major Duncan Heyward and a psalm-singing teacher named David Gamut. Misled by the Huron guide Magua, they are rescued by the scout Hawkeye and his companions Chingachgook and his son Uncas, the last of the Mohican line. The group's journey through a landscape of ambush, siege and pursuit forms the core of the story.

Cooper's book is an adventure tale of chases, captures and daring escapes, but it is also a meditation on the disappearance of Native American peoples and the cost of colonial conflict. His long descriptive passages of rivers, caves and forests helped create a romantic image of the American wilderness. Modern readers often question his portrayals of Native characters, which makes the novel a valuable text for thinking about how myths of the frontier were made.

Published in 1826, it was the second of Cooper's five Leatherstocking Tales featuring the frontiersman Natty Bumppo, known here as Hawkeye. It was popular in America and Europe and shaped the frontier adventure story and the later Western. It has been adapted many times for film, television, radio and comics.
the-three-musketeers: In 1625 a hot-headed young man from Gascony named d'Artagnan arrives in Paris hoping to join the King's Musketeers. On his very first day he manages to challenge three of them to duels: the noble and melancholy Athos, the boastful giant Porthos and the elegant Aramis, who dreams of the priesthood. Instead of fighting each other, they unite against the guards of Cardinal Richelieu, and the four become inseparable. Soon they are drawn into a dangerous intrigue to protect the honour of Queen Anne, which sends them racing across France and to England and brings them up against the mysterious and ruthless Milady.

The novel is a celebration of friendship, courage and loyalty, full of sword fights, disguises, secret letters and narrow escapes. Dumas writes with energy and humour, and his heroes are lively and flawed rather than perfect. The story mixes real historical figures such as Louis XIII, Richelieu and the Duke of Buckingham with invention, making it a gateway to the history of seventeenth-century France.

The Three Musketeers was serialised in the Paris newspaper Le Siècle in 1844, written in collaboration with Auguste Maquet. Its success led to the sequels Twenty Years After and The Vicomte of Bragelonne. It is one of the most adapted French novels, retold in films, television series, animation, comics and stage productions around the world.
the-decameron: The Decameron opens with a vivid description of the plague that struck Florence in 1348. Seven young women and three young men meet in a church and decide to leave the stricken city for the countryside. To pass the time pleasantly, each of them tells one story a day for ten days, producing one hundred tales in all. Each day a member of the group is chosen to rule and usually sets a theme, such as fortune, clever replies, tricks played by wives on husbands, or acts of generosity.

The stories range from bawdy farce and practical jokes to tragic love and moral examples, and they feature merchants, monks, nuns, nobles, peasants and rogues. Boccaccio celebrates wit, intelligence and human desire, and often mocks the hypocrisy of the clergy. The frame of storytellers fleeing a pandemic gives the book a particular resonance today, as a reflection on how stories help people endure fear and loss.

Boccaccio composed the work around 1349 to 1353, writing in Florentine Italian rather than Latin, and it helped establish Italian prose as a literary language. Its frame narrative and many of its plots spread across Europe. Petrarch translated its final tale of patient Griselda into Latin, Chaucer retold it in English, and later writers including Shakespeare drew on its stories. It has also been adapted for film, theatre and illustration.
civil-disobedience: In this short essay Henry David Thoreau asks what a person owes to a government that does wrong. He argues that individual conscience must come before the law, and that citizens should not lend their support to injustice simply because a majority has approved it. Writing at a time when the United States allowed slavery and was fighting a war with Mexico that he opposed, Thoreau says that the honest response is to withdraw cooperation, even if that means going to prison. He describes his own night in the Concord jail after refusing to pay his poll tax, and reflects on the strange freedom he felt there.

The essay is direct, personal and often sharply witty. Its core ideas, that moral responsibility cannot be handed over to the state and that peaceful refusal can be a powerful form of protest, remain at the centre of debates about conscience, law and activism. It is short enough to read in one sitting and rewards discussion.

Thoreau first delivered the material as a lecture in Concord in 1848, and it was published in 1849 under the title Resistance to Civil Government. The better-known title Civil Disobedience was used after his death. The essay went on to influence Leo Tolstoy, Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr., among many others, and it remains a foundational text for movements of nonviolent resistance.
the-wonderful-adventures-of-nils: Nils Holgersson is a fourteen-year-old boy on a farm in Skåne, in the far south of Sweden, who is lazy and cruel to animals. When he mistreats a tomte, a small household spirit, he is shrunk to the size of a thumb and finds he can understand the speech of animals. As a flock of wild geese passes overhead, the family's white farm goose Martin tries to follow them, and Nils, clinging to his neck, is carried into the sky. Led by the wise old goose Akka from Kebnekaise, the flock flies north across the country, and Nils travels with them through a long series of adventures.

The book is both a gripping adventure and a portrait of Sweden's landscapes, provinces, legends and ways of life. Through his journey Nils slowly learns humility, courage and compassion for creatures he once tormented. Lagerlöf blends folklore, natural history and moral growth with gentle humour, creating a story that appeals to children and adults alike.

Lagerlöf was commissioned to write a geography reader for Swedish schoolchildren, and the work appeared in two volumes in 1906 and 1907. It became one of the most famous Swedish books in the world and was translated into many languages. In 1909 Lagerlöf became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. The story has been adapted into films, television series and animation.
oliver-twist: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse, where his mother dies soon after his birth. Raised on meagre rations under the pompous beadle Mr Bumble, he becomes notorious for daring to ask for more food. After a miserable apprenticeship to an undertaker, he runs away to London, where he is taken in by the cheerful Artful Dodger and introduced to Fagin, who trains boys as pickpockets. Oliver's innocence sets him apart from the gang, and his fate becomes a struggle between those who would exploit him, including the violent Bill Sikes, and those who would help him, such as the kindly Mr Brownlow and the conflicted Nancy.

Dickens combined melodrama, suspense, comedy and outrage to expose the cruelty of the workhouse system and the conditions that drove children into crime. His characters are vivid and memorable, and the novel's dark London streets are among his most atmospheric settings. Modern readers also note, and debate, the antisemitic portrayal of Fagin, which Dickens himself later softened in revised editions.

The novel was serialised in Bentley's Miscellany from 1837 and published in book form in 1838, with illustrations by George Cruikshank. Written in response to the New Poor Law of 1834, it established Dickens as a social novelist. It has been adapted many times for film, television and stage, including a celebrated musical.
persuasion: Anne Elliot is twenty-seven, the overlooked middle daughter of the vain and extravagant Sir Walter Elliot. Eight years earlier she was engaged to a young naval officer, Frederick Wentworth, but was persuaded by her trusted friend Lady Russell to break it off because he lacked fortune and connections. Now her father's debts force the family to let their estate, Kellynch Hall, and the new tenants turn out to be Wentworth's sister and her husband. Wentworth, now a wealthy captain after the Napoleonic Wars, returns to the neighbourhood, and Anne must face him again as the story moves between the countryside, the seaside at Lyme Regis and the society of Bath.

Austen's final completed novel is quieter and more reflective than her earlier work. It explores regret, constancy, the passing of youth and the question of when it is right to yield to advice. Its admiration for the self-made naval officers contrasts with its satire of snobbish rank. Anne's inner life is drawn with great delicacy, making this a favourite among readers who value emotional depth.

Austen finished the novel in 1816 and died in July 1817. It was published posthumously in December 1817, alongside Northanger Abbey, with a biographical notice by her brother Henry. Manuscript chapters showing her revision of the ending survive. It has been adapted for television, film, radio and the stage.
mrs-dalloway: The novel follows a single day in June 1923 in London. Clarissa Dalloway, the wife of a Conservative member of Parliament, walks out to buy flowers for the party she is giving that evening. As she moves through the city, her thoughts drift back to her youth at Bourton, to her old suitor Peter Walsh, who unexpectedly reappears that morning, and to her friend Sally Seton. Running alongside her story is that of Septimus Warren Smith, a young veteran of the First World War suffering from shell shock, and his Italian wife Lucrezia, who are seeking help from doctors who barely understand him.

Woolf moves fluidly in and out of the minds of many characters, linking them through shared moments such as the striking of Big Ben. The book explores time and memory, the aftermath of war, mental illness, social class and the hidden depths behind ordinary lives. Its lyrical, flowing style rewards slow reading and shows how much can happen within an apparently uneventful day.

Mrs Dalloway was published in 1925 by the Hogarth Press, which Woolf ran with her husband Leonard. It is regarded as one of the central works of literary modernism. Woolf's working title was The Hours, a phrase Michael Cunningham later used for his own novel inspired by the book. It has also been adapted for film and the stage.
the-canterbury-tales: On a spring day, a group of about thirty pilgrims gathers at the Tabard Inn in Southwark, ready to travel to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury. The innkeeper, Harry Bailly, proposes a contest: each pilgrim will tell stories on the journey, and the best teller will win a free supper. The General Prologue introduces the company, including the Knight, the Miller, the Prioress, the Wife of Bath, the Pardoner and many more, and the tales that follow range from courtly romance and saints' lives to sermons, fables and riotous comic stories.

Chaucer gives each pilgrim a distinctive voice, so that the tales reveal as much about their tellers as about their subjects. The work offers a lively cross-section of medieval society and its attitudes to love, marriage, religion, money and power, often with sharp irony toward hypocrisy. Its humour, its range of styles and its gallery of characters make it as entertaining as it is historically revealing.

Chaucer worked on the collection from the late 1380s until his death in 1400, and it was left unfinished, with only some of the planned tales completed. Written in Middle English, it helped establish English as a language of serious literature. It survives in many manuscripts and was among the early books printed in England by William Caxton. It has inspired modernisations, stage versions, films and television retellings.
the-brothers-karamazov: In a small Russian town, the dissolute and greedy landowner Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov lives in open conflict with his sons. Dmitri, the eldest, is passionate and reckless, and quarrels with his father over money and over the same woman, Grushenka. Ivan is a brilliant intellectual tormented by the question of how a good God can allow suffering. Alyosha, the youngest, is a gentle novice at the local monastery under the wise Elder Zosima. Also in the household is the servant Smerdyakov, rumoured to be another son. As tensions rise, a violent crime throws the family into crisis and sets in motion an investigation and trial.

The novel is at once a family drama, a murder mystery and a profound debate about faith, doubt, freedom and moral responsibility. Its most famous chapter, The Grand Inquisitor, presents Ivan's parable of Christ returning during the Spanish Inquisition. Dostoevsky gives powerful voice to belief and unbelief alike, and his intense, feverish characters remain unforgettable.

The Brothers Karamazov was serialised in the journal The Russian Messenger in 1879 and 1880, and Dostoevsky died only a few months after its completion. It is widely regarded as his greatest work and has influenced novelists, philosophers, theologians and psychologists. It has been adapted for film, television and the stage in Russia and elsewhere.
germinal: Étienne Lantier, an unemployed young mechanic, arrives on a cold night at the coal-mining town of Montsou in northern France. He finds work at the Voreux pit and lodges with the Maheu family, whose members of every age labour underground for wages that barely keep them alive. Étienne grows close to the Maheus and especially to their daughter Catherine. Angered by the miners' poverty and influenced by socialist ideas, he becomes a leader among them, and when the company cuts their pay, the community is drawn into a long and desperate strike.

Zola portrays the physical reality of mining, the darkness, danger and exhaustion, with overwhelming force, and contrasts the miners' hunger with the comfort of the shareholders and managers. The novel explores class conflict, the rival paths of reform and revolution, and the power of collective action, while showing sympathy for characters on many sides. Its themes of exploitation and solidarity remain highly relevant.

Published in 1885, Germinal is the thirteenth novel in Zola's twenty-volume Rougon-Macquart cycle. Zola researched it closely, visiting the mining region around Anzin. Its title refers to a spring month in the French Republican calendar, suggesting new growth. It is often considered his masterpiece and has been adapted for film, television and the stage.
andersen-s-fairy-tales: This collection gathers the stories of Hans Christian Andersen, who was born in the Danish town of Odense in 1805 and became one of the most beloved storytellers in the world. Among them are The Little Mermaid, about a sea princess who longs for a human soul; The Ugly Duckling, about a mocked outsider; The Snow Queen, in which the brave girl Gerda sets out to rescue her friend Kai; The Emperor's New Clothes, The Princess and the Pea, The Steadfast Tin Soldier and The Little Match Girl. Some draw on folk tales Andersen heard as a child, but many are his own inventions.

Andersen's tales are often playful and humorous, yet many carry deep melancholy, exploring loneliness, longing, vanity, faith and the gap between outward appearances and true worth. He wrote in a lively, conversational style that sounds like spoken storytelling, and he frequently gave voices to everyday objects and animals. The stories speak to children and adults on different levels.

Andersen published his first small booklet of tales for children in 1835 and continued writing new ones for decades. They were soon translated across Europe and have since appeared in a great many languages. The stories have inspired countless picture books, ballets, operas, animated films and stage works, and the statue of the Little Mermaid in Copenhagen has become a symbol of the city.
war-and-peace: War and Peace follows a handful of Russian aristocratic families, chiefly the Rostovs and Bolkonskys, from 1805 through Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 and beyond. At its heart are three young people: the awkward, searching Pierre Bezukhov, the proud and disillusioned Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, and the lively Natasha Rostova. Their friendships, engagements, quarrels and losses play out in Moscow and St Petersburg drawing rooms, on country estates and on the battlefields of Austerlitz and Borodino, while Napoleon and the Russian commander Kutuzov appear in person.

Tolstoy weaves private life and public history so closely that each lights up the other. The novel asks what gives a life meaning, how people change, and whether great men truly steer events or are carried along by forces larger than themselves; Tolstoy even interrupts the story with essays on the nature of history. Its scenes of balls, hunts and battles are written with astonishing clarity. Long as it is, it gives a rare sense of having lived alongside an entire society.

Parts of the work first appeared in instalments in The Russian Messenger from 1865 under the title 1805, and the complete novel was published as a book in 1869. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest novels ever written and helped establish Tolstoy's international reputation. Its scale has inspired an opera by Sergei Prokofiev and numerous film, television and stage adaptations.
frankenstein: Frankenstein opens with letters from Robert Walton, an Arctic explorer who takes aboard a half-frozen stranger named Victor Frankenstein. Victor tells his story: a gifted young man from Geneva, he becomes obsessed at university with discovering the secret of life, and succeeds in animating a creature built from dead matter. Horrified by what he has made, he flees from it. The creature, left alone in a hostile world, learns language and feeling by secretly observing a family, and eventually confronts its maker with demands of its own.

Mary Shelley's novel is far more than a horror story. It explores the dangers of unchecked scientific ambition, the duties a creator owes to what he creates, and the way rejection and loneliness can twist a sensitive being. Unusually, the creature is given a voice of its own, eloquent and moving, which complicates any simple idea of who the real monster is. Its urgent moral questions feel fresh in an age of genetic engineering and artificial intelligence.

The novel grew out of a ghost-story challenge among Mary Shelley, Percy Bysshe Shelley and Lord Byron near Lake Geneva in 1816. Subtitled The Modern Prometheus, it was published anonymously in London in 1818, and a revised edition followed in 1831. It is often called one of the first works of science fiction. Stage versions appeared within a few years, and countless adaptations have followed.
the-phantom-of-the-opera: The Phantom of the Opera is set in the Paris Opera House in the late nineteenth century, whose cellars descend to an underground lake. The new managers inherit strange rumours of an Opera Ghost who demands a private box and a monthly salary, and accidents seem to follow whenever his wishes are ignored. Meanwhile Christine Daaé, a modest Swedish singer, suddenly blossoms into a sensational talent, crediting a mysterious Angel of Music who teaches her through the walls. Her childhood friend, the young Viscount Raoul de Chagny, becomes determined to uncover who this invisible tutor really is.

Leroux, a former journalist, presents the story as an investigation, mixing documents, testimonies and the narrator's own inquiries. The result blends Gothic horror, romance, mystery and backstage comedy. At its centre is a figure both terrifying and pitiable, a genius shut out from ordinary life by his appearance, which gives the novel its lasting emotional pull. Its atmosphere and suspense remain irresistible.

The novel was first serialised in the French newspaper Le Gaulois in 1909 and 1910 and published as a book in 1910. Its fame grew enormously through adaptation. A celebrated silent film version appeared in the 1920s, and the story was later turned into one of the most successful stage musicals ever produced, along with many other films, television versions and stage works.
the-count-of-monte-cristo: The Count of Monte Cristo begins in Marseille in 1815. Edmond Dantès, a young and honest sailor, is about to become a ship's captain and marry his beloved Mercédès when jealous rivals and an ambitious public prosecutor conspire against him. Accused of supporting the exiled Napoleon, he is thrown without trial into the grim island fortress of the Château d'If. There, after years of despair, he befriends a fellow prisoner, the learned Abbé Faria, who educates him and reveals the location of a hidden treasure. Years later a wealthy and enigmatic count appears in Parisian high society with plans of his own.

Dumas built a sprawling adventure full of disguises, intrigue, poisonings, duels and dramatic reversals, but the novel is also a serious meditation on justice, revenge, forgiveness and the limits of human power. Its pace and inventiveness make it gripping, while its portrait of corruption in banking, the law and politics under the Restoration and July Monarchy still feels pointed.

The novel was serialised in the Journal des Débats between 1844 and 1846, with Dumas working alongside his collaborator Auguste Maquet. It was hugely popular in France and was quickly translated across Europe and beyond. It remains one of the most widely read adventure novels in the world and has inspired many stage, film, television and comic-book adaptations, as well as countless revenge stories.
faust: Goethe's Faust is a drama in verse built on the old German legend of a scholar who sells his soul to the devil. It opens with a prologue in heaven, where Mephistopheles wagers with the Lord that he can lead the learned Doctor Faust astray. On earth, Faust is in despair: he has mastered philosophy, law, medicine and theology, yet feels he knows nothing that matters. Mephistopheles appears and the two strike a bargain: the devil will serve Faust and show him every pleasure, and if Faust ever finds a moment so satisfying that he wishes it to last, his soul will be forfeit. Part One centres on Faust's love affair with the young Gretchen; Part Two ranges through imperial courts, classical myth and grand public projects.

The play explores striving, desire, knowledge and the restless modern spirit that is never content. It mixes tragedy, comedy, lyric poetry and philosophy, and its language is among the richest in German literature.

Goethe worked on Faust for some sixty years. Part One was published in 1808, and Part Two appeared in 1832, shortly after his death. The work became a cornerstone of German culture and inspired composers such as Gounod, Berlioz and Liszt, along with countless stage productions, translations and reworkings.
capital-volume-i: Capital, Volume I is Karl Marx's major analysis of how capitalist economies work. It begins with the commodity, the basic unit of wealth in a market society, and distinguishes between its usefulness and its exchange value. From there Marx examines money, then asks how capital grows. His answer centres on labour-power: workers sell their capacity to work for a wage, but produce more value than they are paid, and this surplus value is the source of profit. The book goes on to study the length of the working day, the rise of factories and machinery, wages, the accumulation of capital, and the often violent separation of people from the land.

Marx combines economic theory with history, philosophy and detailed evidence from British government reports on factory conditions, child labour and public health. Ideas such as commodity fetishism and surplus value have shaped debates far beyond economics. Agree or not, readers gain a powerful lens on work and inequality.

The volume was first published in German in Hamburg in 1867. Marx did not live to finish the later volumes, which Friedrich Engels edited from his manuscripts and published in 1885 and 1894. An English translation appeared in 1887. Capital became the foundational text of Marxist thought and influenced political movements, governments and scholarship in sociology, history and economics around the world.
extraordinary-popular-delusions-and-the-: Charles Mackay, a Scottish journalist, set out to chronicle the strange ideas and enthusiasms that have gripped whole populations at once. The best-known chapters deal with financial manias: John Law's Mississippi Scheme in France, the South Sea Bubble in England, and the craze for tulip bulbs in the seventeenth-century Netherlands. But Mackay ranges much further, covering alchemists and fortune-tellers, the witch trials, the Crusades, prophecies of the end of the world, magnetisers, fashions in hair and beards, duels, the veneration of relics, and popular admiration for highwaymen.

Running through the book is a single idea: people, as Mackay saw it, think in herds, and become foolish together in ways they would never be alone, recovering their senses only slowly and one by one. His style is brisk, ironic and anecdotal, which makes the book entertaining to dip into. Modern historians have questioned some of his accounts, particularly the scale of the tulip mania, so it is best read as lively popular history rather than a precise record. Its warnings about speculation and mass enthusiasm still feel strikingly relevant.

The book first appeared in London in 1841 under the title Memoirs of Extraordinary Popular Delusions, and later editions adopted the longer title by which it is now known. It has stayed in print and is frequently recommended to investors and cited in discussions of market bubbles and crowd behaviour.
common-sense: Common Sense is a political pamphlet that argued, at a moment when many colonists still hoped for reconciliation with Britain, that the American colonies should declare full independence. Thomas Paine begins by distinguishing society, which arises from human needs, from government, which he calls at best a necessary evil. He then attacks monarchy and hereditary succession as absurd and unjust, questions the value of the British connection, argues that it is unnatural for a small island to govern a vast continent, and sets out the practical reasons why the colonies could succeed on their own.

What made the pamphlet so effective was its voice. Paine wrote in direct, vigorous language for ordinary readers rather than lawyers and scholars, drawing on everyday reasoning and familiar Biblical references. Reading it today offers a vivid sense of how political argument can move public opinion, and it remains a striking example of persuasive writing about liberty, consent and the purpose of government.

Paine, who had arrived in America from England only in late 1774, published the pamphlet anonymously in Philadelphia in January 1776. It was widely reprinted, read aloud and discussed throughout the colonies, and is generally credited with strengthening support for independence in the months before the Declaration of Independence that July. It remains one of the most influential pamphlets in American history and is still widely taught.
the-secret-garden: The Secret Garden begins in India, where Mary Lennox, a sour, neglected girl, is orphaned by an outbreak of cholera. She is sent to England to live with her uncle, Archibald Craven, at Misselthwaite Manor, a huge, gloomy house on the Yorkshire moors. Her uncle is mostly absent and the house is full of locked rooms. Through the cheerful housemaid Martha, the gruff old gardener Ben Weatherstaff, and a friendly robin, Mary learns of a walled garden that has been shut up for ten years. Curious for the first time in her life, she begins searching for a way in, while puzzling over the strange crying she hears in the night.

The novel is a story of healing: of children, of a family, and of a neglected place. Burnett celebrates fresh air, outdoor work, friendship and the power of nature and positive thinking, and her characters grow in believable, touching ways. The garden's changing seasons mirror the children's growth, and the Yorkshire speech of Martha and her brother Dickon adds warmth.

The story was serialised in The American Magazine from 1910 to 1911 and published as a book in 1911. It drew less attention at first than Burnett's earlier Little Lord Fauntleroy, but its reputation grew steadily over the following century, and it is now regarded as a classic of children's literature, adapted many times for screen and stage.
the-time-machine: The Time Machine opens at a dinner party in Richmond, where a scientist known only as the Time Traveller explains to his sceptical guests that time is a fourth dimension through which a person might move. A week later he arrives late and dishevelled, and tells them what happened when he tested his machine. He travelled to the year 802,701, where he found a seemingly peaceful world inhabited by the Eloi, small, gentle and childlike people who live among ruined buildings and fruit gardens. But when his machine goes missing, he begins to suspect that this paradise conceals something darker beneath the ground.

Wells used the story to imagine humanity's future. The split between the Eloi and the Morlocks reflects his concerns about the class divisions of Victorian England and about evolution, which need not always mean progress. Short and fast-moving, it combines adventure with speculation, and its images of a far future have lost little of their power.

The novella was published in 1895 and was Wells's first major success, soon followed by The Invisible Man and The War of the Worlds. It popularised the idea of a machine that lets a person travel through time at will, and it is widely seen as a founding work of modern science fiction. It has been adapted for film, television and radio, and countless time-travel stories owe it a debt.
madame-bovary: Madame Bovary tells the story of Emma Rouault, a farmer's daughter in Normandy who has filled her head with romantic novels and dreams of passion, elegance and Parisian life. She marries Charles Bovary, a kind but dull country doctor, and quickly finds married life in a small provincial town unbearably flat. A glimpse of aristocratic luxury at a ball sharpens her discontent. After the couple move to the market town of Yonville, Emma seeks escape through love affairs and through spending, encouraged by a scheming draper, and her choices draw her into ever deeper trouble.

Flaubert treats his heroine with a mixture of irony and sympathy, showing how the clichés of romance and the narrowness of bourgeois life both trap her. He famously laboured over every sentence, and his precise, controlled prose and use of free indirect style, which lets narration slip into a character's thoughts, influenced generations of novelists. The book remains a sharp study of desire, consumerism, boredom and self-deception.

The novel was first serialised in the Revue de Paris in 1856, even though the magazine cut some passages. Early in 1857 Flaubert, the magazine's editor and its printer were tried for offending public morals and were acquitted, and the novel appeared as a book that year, helped by the publicity. It is now considered a masterpiece of realism and has been adapted many times for film, television and the stage.
metamorphoses: Metamorphoses is a long narrative poem in fifteen books, written in Latin hexameter by the Roman poet Ovid. Its subject is change of shape. Beginning with the creation of the world out of chaos, it moves through the ages of humankind, the flood and hundreds of myths in which gods and mortals are transformed: Daphne into a laurel tree, Narcissus into a flower, Arachne into a spider. Stories of Phaethon, Pyramus and Thisbe, Orpheus and Eurydice, and Pygmalion flow into one another, before the poem passes through the Trojan War and the legends of Rome to reach Julius Caesar and Ovid's own time.

Ovid's tone is playful, witty and often unsettling, shifting between humour, eroticism, cruelty and pathos. He is fascinated by desire, power, the arbitrary behaviour of the gods and the fragile boundary between human and natural worlds. His skill in linking tales together keeps the poem moving, and it remains one of the best ways to discover the stories of classical mythology.

Ovid completed the poem around 8 AD, the year he was exiled by the emperor Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea. Widely read through the Middle Ages and Renaissance, it became one of the most influential works in Western culture, shaping writers such as Chaucer and Shakespeare, as well as painters such as Titian. Modern poets continue to translate and retell it.
the-prince-and-the-pauper: The Prince and the Pauper is set in London in 1547, at the end of the reign of Henry VIII. Tom Canty is a beggar boy from the slums of Offal Court, who dreams of royal life. Edward, Prince of Wales, the king's young son, lives amid every luxury. When chance brings the two boys face to face inside the palace grounds, they discover they look almost exactly alike and, on a whim, exchange clothes. Before they can switch back, the prince is thrown out of the gates as a ragged pauper, while Tom is left to play the heir to the throne, with no one believing either of them.

Twain uses this simple premise to explore injustice, cruelty in the law, and the gap between rulers and the ruled. Edward, wandering among thieves and vagrants with the help of a loyal soldier, Miles Hendon, learns how harshly ordinary people are treated, while Tom struggles with the strange burdens of court life. The book blends comedy, adventure and sharp social criticism.

Published in 1881, it was Twain's first historical novel and was aimed at younger readers as well as adults. It marked a change from the American settings of his earlier work and was well received. The story of identical strangers swapping places has been adapted many times for stage, film, television and animation.
anne-of-green-gables: Anne of Green Gables is set in the small farming community of Avonlea on Prince Edward Island. Matthew Cuthbert and his sister Marilla, an unmarried pair getting on in years, decide to adopt an orphan boy to help on their farm, Green Gables. Instead, a mix-up brings them Anne Shirley, a red-haired, freckled eleven-year-old girl who talks almost without stopping, gives romantic names to everything she sees and longs above all for a real home. Marilla's first instinct is to send her back, but Anne's charm begins to work on both of them, and the novel follows her schooldays, friendships and many comic scrapes.

Montgomery's novel celebrates imagination, kindness and the joy of belonging. Anne's mistakes are funny and her feelings are vivid, and readers watch her grow through friendship with her bosom friend Diana Barry and rivalry with her classmate Gilbert Blythe. The island's landscapes are described with real love, and the book's gentle humour and warmth appeal to adults as much as children.

The novel was published in 1908 and was an immediate success, leading Montgomery to write several sequels following Anne into adulthood. It is one of the best-known works of Canadian literature, has been translated into many languages, and has drawn visitors to Prince Edward Island for generations. It has been adapted for film, television, animation and the stage, including a long-running musical in Canada.
a-tale-of-two-cities: A Tale of Two Cities moves between London and Paris in the years before and during the French Revolution. It opens in 1775 as Lucie Manette learns that her father, a French doctor she believed dead, has been released after eighteen years of secret imprisonment in the Bastille. Their lives become tied to two very different men: Charles Darnay, a French aristocrat who has rejected his family's cruelty, and Sydney Carton, a brilliant but dissolute English lawyer who scorns himself. Meanwhile, in the Paris wine shop of Monsieur and Madame Defarge, the anger of the poor is gathering towards revolution.

Dickens explores injustice and its consequences, showing how aristocratic oppression breeds revolutionary violence, and how both can crush individuals. Against this he sets loyalty, love and the possibility of redemption. The novel is more tightly plotted than many of his books, with dramatic set pieces, memorable villains and a famous opening that begins, It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.

The novel was published in weekly instalments in Dickens's new magazine All the Year Round between April and November 1859, and as a book the same year. Dickens drew on Thomas Carlyle's history of the French Revolution. It is among his most widely read works and has been adapted many times for stage, film, radio and television.
tess-of-the-d-urbervilles: Tess of the d'Urbervilles takes place in Wessex, Thomas Hardy's fictional version of rural south-west England. John Durbeyfield, a poor and idle haggler, or pedlar, learns from a parson that his family is descended from the ancient Norman line of the d'Urbervilles. Hoping to profit from the connection, the family sends their eldest daughter, Tess, to seek help from a wealthy household bearing the d'Urberville name. There she meets Alec, the family's arrogant son, and an encounter with him shapes the rest of her life. Later, working as a dairymaid, she meets Angel Clare, a thoughtful clergyman's son, and must decide what she owes to her own past.

Hardy's novel is a powerful protest against the double standards of Victorian morality, which judged women harshly for what was done to them. It also mourns a changing countryside, as old rural ways give way to machinery and migration. Its descriptions of landscape, seasons and farm work are among the finest in English fiction, and Tess herself remains one of literature's most moving heroines.

The novel was first serialised in censored form in the illustrated newspaper The Graphic in 1891, and was published in full as a book that year, subtitled A Pure Woman Faithfully Presented.
